title: Names of the days of the week
wiki_lead:
In a vast number of languages, the names given to the seven days of the week are derived from the names of the seven classical planets which were in turn named after contemporary Hellenistic deities. This system was introduced by the Sumerians and later adopted by the Babylonians from whom the Roman Empire adopted the system during late antiquity. In some other languages, the days are named after corresponding deities of the regional culture, such as the Germanic deities reflected in the English weekdays.
The seven-day week was adopted in early Christianity from the Hebrew calendar, and gradually replaced the Roman internundinum. Eight-day and seven-day weeks existed side-by-side until the Emperor Constantine made the seven-day week official in AD 321; thereafter, the seven-day week spread throughout the Roman Empire and eventually through Christian cultures around the world.
The history of the seven-day week can be traced to ancient civilizations. Sunday remained the first day of the week, being considered the day of the sun god Sol Invictus and the Lord's Day, while the Jewish Sabbath remained the seventh. Most historians agree the seven-day week dates back to Babylonians who started using it about 4,000 years ago. The number 7 was sacred to the Babylonians. Emperor Constantine of the Roman Empire made the Day of the Sun (dies Solis, "Sunday") a legal holiday centuries later.
In the international standard ISO 8601, Monday is treated as the first day of the week, but in many countries it is counted as the second day of the week.

Days named after planets


Greco-Roman tradition

Between the first and third centuries AD, the Roman Empire gradually replaced the eight-day Roman nundinal cycle with the seven-day week. The earliest evidence for this new system is a Pompeiian graffito referring to 6 February 60 AD (ante diem viii idus Februarias) as dies solis ("Sunday"). Another early witness is a reference to a lost treatise by Plutarch, written in about 100 AD, which addressed the question of: "Why are the days named after the planets reckoned in a different order from the 'actual' order?" The treatise is lost, but the answer to the question is known; see planetary hours.
The Ptolemaic system of planetary spheres asserts that the order of the heavenly bodies from the farthest to the closest to the Earth is Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon; objectively, the planets are ordered from slowest to fastest moving as they appear in the night sky.
The days were named after the classical planets of Hellenistic astrology, in the order: Sun (Helios), Moon (Selene), Mars (Ares), Mercury (Hermes), Jupiter (Zeus), Venus (Aphrodite), and Saturn (Cronus).

grok_lead: The names of the days of the week refer to the linguistic labels assigned to the seven consecutive days in a standard weekly cycle, which vary significantly across cultures but frequently draw from astronomical observations, deities, or numerical sequences. In many Western traditions, these names trace back to the planetary week system of ancient Hellenistic astrology, where each day was associated with one of the seven visible celestial bodiesâSaturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon âordered according to their perceived geocentric distances or mythological hierarchies. This framework, which emerged around the 1st or 2nd century BCE in the Mediterranean world, spread through trade, conquest, and religious adoption, influencing calendars from Europe to Asia. In the Roman tradition, the days were named after these celestial bodies or their corresponding gods, using genitive forms in Latin: dies Solis (day of the Sun) for Sunday, dies Lunae (day of the Moon) for Monday, dies Martis (day of Mars) for Tuesday, dies Mercurii (day of Mercury) for Wednesday, dies Iovis (day of Jupiter) for Thursday, dies Veneris (day of Venus) for Friday, and dies Saturni (day of Saturn) for Saturday. These designations reflected astrological beliefs linking planetary influences to daily affairs, with the sequence determined by the Chaldean order of planets descending from Saturn. The seven-day structure itself likely has roots in earlier Mesopotamian or Judeo-Babylonian lunar calendars, where cycles of seven aligned with phases of the Moon, and was widespread in the Roman Empire by the 3rd century CE and officially recognized under Emperor Constantine in the 4th century CE, who elevated Sunday as a day of rest in 321 CE. As the Roman planetary week disseminated northward, Germanic tribes adapted the names by substituting Roman deities with their own pagan gods, preserving the celestial associations while infusing local mythology; for instance, Mars became Tiw (a war god), Mercury became Woden (chief of the gods, akin to Odin), Jupiter became Thunor (thunder god, akin to Thor), and Venus became Frigg (goddess of love and marriage). This resulted in the modern English names: Sunday (Sun's day), Monday (Moon's day), Tuesday (Tiw's day), Wednesday (Woden's day), Thursday (Thunor's day), Friday (Frigg's day), and Saturday (retaining the Roman Saturn). Christianization efforts from the 3rd to 7th centuries CE further reshaped the system in Europe, with early Church fathers like those in Greek traditions accommodating planetary names while Latin authorities sought to suppress pagan connotations, ultimately integrating the week into the liturgical calendar without fully eradicating the astrological roots. Beyond Indo-European languages, naming conventions diverge markedly; for example, Romance languages like French and Spanish largely retain Latin planetary roots ( lundi for Moon's day, mardi for Mars's day), while East Asian systems vary; Chinese uses numerical designations (e.g., "week one" to "week seven"), while Japanese employs names derived from celestial bodies and the five elements (e.g., "Moon day" for Monday). Indigenous traditions, like those of the Navajo, employ descriptive numerical phrases based on ordinal positions from Sunday, and ancient Mesoamerican cultures such as the Aztecs used a 13-day cycle with unique symbolic names unrelated to planets. The global standardization of the seven-day week, including its names, accelerated through colonialism, missionary work, and international commerce, making it a cornerstone of modern calendars worldwide despite these cultural variations.
